newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Annan to support Malaysian in major libel case.
newsitem.headline: Annan to support Malaysian in major libel case.

text.p: U.N. human rights investigators on Friday closed ranks around a Malaysian colleague, urging U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to take further steps to protect his immunity from a $25 million libel suit.
In a joint letter, the 30 experts argued that immunity from legal process granted to U.N. specialists under a 1946 convention had been undermined by the Malaysian courts.
"They will have no difficulty getting that from the secretary-general, who feels strong about this matter," said U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard in New York. "It is a matter of principle."
Eckhard did not say what Annan would do. However, U.N. sources said officials were consulting with Malaysia, including Razali Ismail, its U.N. envoy and this year's General Assembly president.

A Malaysian High Court last month allowed a libel suit by two Malaysian companies to proceed against Param Cumaraswamy, a Malaysian lawyer who serves as U.N. special rapporteur (investigator) on the Independence of Judges and Lawyers.

MBf Capital Bhd and MBf Northern Securities Sdn Bhd alleged Cumaraswamy had defamed them in an article published in the November 1995 issue of the International Commercial Litigation magazine, a London-based publication.
In the article, Cumaraswamy was quoted as saying he was investigating complaints that businessmen were manipulating the Malaysian judicial system.
U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Ralph Zacklin said that the world body regarded the matter with the "utmost seriousness and urgency."

Annan waded into the lawsuit last March, submitting a certificate to the court asserting Cumaraswamy enjoyed the protections provided under the Convention on Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations.
The rapporteurs -- who investigate allegations in countries including Burma, Iran and Nigeria -- wrote Annan "asking for a further affirmation of the immunity of the Special Rapporteurs."

"Threatening the immunity of one expert constitutes an attack on the entire system and institution of the United Nations special (human rights) procedures and mechanisms," the human rights envoys said.
Their letter stopped short of calls by some non-governmental organisations urging Annan to immediately bring the case of Cumaraswamy's immunity to the International Court of Justice.
On June 28, Malayia's Judicial Commissioner Zainun Ali dismissed with costs Cumaraswamy's application to strike out the 60 million ringgit ($23.8 million) suit by the two firms.
She ordered him to file and serve his defence within 14 days, but said he could cite evidence at the trial to support his claim of immunity, according to Malaysia's New Sunday Times.
